title: Complex Numbers
description: Cartesian form, Argand diagrams, modulus and argument, polar and Euler forms, and the geometry of complex operations.

notes.heading: Introduction to Complex Numbers & Cartesian Form
notes.body:
Complex numbers extend the real number system so that every quadratic equation has a solution. They are built from a real part and an imaginary part linked by the special number $i$.

📌 Definition of the Imaginary Unit
$i$ is defined by the property:
    $$i^2 = -1$$
This means the square root of any negative number can be rewritten:
    $$\sqrt{-a} = i\sqrt{a}$$     (for $a > 0$)

📌 Cartesian Form
A complex number $z$ is written as:
    $$z = a + bi$$
where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.
• $a = \operatorname{Re}(z)$ is the real part
• $b = \operatorname{Im}(z)$ is the imaginary part

Two complex numbers are equal only when both their real parts and their imaginary parts match.

🔑 Addition & Subtraction
Combine the real and imaginary parts separately:
    $$(a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + c) + (b + d)i$$
    $$(a + bi) - (c + di) = (a - c) + (b - d)i$$

🔑 Multiplication in Cartesian Form
Expand just like algebraic brackets, replacing $i^2$ with $-1$:
    $$(a + bi)(c + di) = ac + adi + bci + bdi^2$$
    $$= (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i$$

💡 Worked Example — Multiplication
Simplify $(2 + 3i)(1 - i)$.

  Step 1: Expand the brackets
    $$2 - 2i + 3i - 3i^2$$

  Step 2: Replace $i^2$ with $-1$
    $$2 + i - 3(-1)$$

  Step 3: Simplify
    $$2 + i + 3 = 5 + i$$

🔑 Powers of $i$
The powers of $i$ repeat every four steps:
    $$i^1 = i$$
    $$i^2 = -1$$
    $$i^3 = -i$$
    $$i^4 = 1$$

To simplify a higher power, divide the exponent by $4$ and use the remainder:
    $$i^{23} = i^{4 \times 5 + 3} = (i^4)^5 \cdot i^3 = 1^5 \cdot (-i) = -i$$

💡 Worked Example — Higher Power of $i$
Simplify $i^{38}$.

  Step 1: Divide $38$ by $4$
    $$38 = 4 \times 9 + 2$$, so the remainder is $2$

  Step 2: Use the cycle
    $$i^{38} = i^2 = -1$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always replace $i^2$ with $-1$ before collecting terms
• Multiplication of two complex numbers always gives another complex number
• For higher powers of $i$, look for the remainder when dividing by $4$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing $\sqrt{-a} \cdot \sqrt{-b} = \sqrt{ab}$. This is only true for real numbers. With negatives:
    $$\sqrt{-4} \times \sqrt{-9} = (2i)(3i) = 6i^2 = -6$$,   not $$\sqrt{36} = 6$$

notes.heading: Complex Conjugates, Division & Modulus
notes.body:
The complex conjugate is a powerful tool that turns division into a simple fraction with a real denominator. It is also closely tied to the modulus, which measures the size of a complex number.

📌 Complex Conjugate
For $z = a + bi$, the conjugate is:
    $$z^* = a - bi$$

🔑 Key Properties of the Conjugate
    $$z + z^* = 2a \quad \text{(always real)}$$
    $$z - z^* = 2bi \quad \text{(always imaginary)}$$
    $$zz^* = a^2 + b^2 \quad \text{(always real and equal to } |z|^2\text{)}$$

📌 Modulus
The modulus $|z|$ is the distance from the origin to $z$ on an Argand diagram:
    $$|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$$

The modulus is never negative. It links directly to the conjugate through:
    $$zz^* = |z|^2$$

🔑 Division Method
To divide two complex numbers:
1. Write the calculation as a single fraction
2. Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator
3. Expand and simplify — the denominator becomes real
4. Write the result in Cartesian form

    $$\dfrac{a + bi}{c + di} = \dfrac{(a + bi)(c - di)}{c^2 + d^2}$$

💡 Worked Example — Division
Simplify $(1 + 7i) \div (3 - i)$.

  Step 1: Write as a fraction
    $$\dfrac{1 + 7i}{3 - i}$$

  Step 2: Multiply top and bottom by $(3 + i)$
    $$\dfrac{(1 + 7i)(3 + i)}{(3 - i)(3 + i)}$$

  Step 3: Expand numerator and denominator
    Numerator: $3 + i + 21i + 7i^2 = 3 + 22i - 7 = -4 + 22i$
    Denominator: $9 + 3i - 3i - i^2 = 9 + 1 = 10$

  Step 4: Simplify
    $$\dfrac{-4 + 22i}{10} = -0.4 + 2.2i$$

💡 Worked Example — Using $zz^* = |z|^2$
If $z = 3 + 4i$, find $z \cdot z^*$.

  Step 1: Identify $a$ and $b$
    $$a = 3, \ b = 4$$

  Step 2: Apply the formula
    $$zz^* = a^2 + b^2 = 9 + 16 = 25$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part only
• $zz^*$ always gives a real number — this is why it removes $i$ from a denominator
• $|z_1 + z_2|$ is not the same as $|z_1| + |z_2|$ in general

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to multiply both numerator and denominator by the conjugate. If you only multiply the top, you have changed the value of the expression.

notes.heading: Argand Diagrams & Argument
notes.body:
An Argand diagram turns complex numbers into geometry. Once you can visualise them as points or vectors, operations like addition and multiplication become much easier to understand.

📌 Argand Diagram
A complex plane with:
• Horizontal axis = real axis ($\text{Re}$)
• Vertical axis = imaginary axis ($\text{Im}$)

The number $z = x + iy$ is plotted at the point $(x, y)$ or drawn as a vector from the origin to that point.

📌 Argument $\arg(z)$
The argument is the angle measured counter-clockwise from the positive real axis to the vector. It is usually given in the range:
    $$-\pi < \arg(z) \leq \pi$$

To calculate it, first find the acute reference angle using:
    $$\text{reference angle} = \tan^{-1}\left(\left|\dfrac{y}{x}\right|\right)$$

Then adjust for the quadrant:
• Q1 ($x > 0$, $y > 0$):   $\arg(z) = \text{reference angle}$
• Q2 ($x < 0$, $y > 0$):   $\arg(z) = \pi - \text{reference angle}$
• Q3 ($x < 0$, $y < 0$):   $\arg(z) = -\pi + \text{reference angle}$
• Q4 ($x > 0$, $y < 0$):   $\arg(z) = -\text{reference angle}$

💡 Worked Example — Finding the Argument
Find $\arg(z)$ for $z = -1 - i$.

  Step 1: Identify the quadrant
    $x = -1$, $y = -1$ → Q3

  Step 2: Find the reference angle
    $$\tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$$

  Step 3: Apply the Q3 rule
    $$\arg(z) = -\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$

🔑 Geometric Operations
• Adding $w$ to $z$ translates $z$ by the vector $(\operatorname{Re}(w), \operatorname{Im}(w))$
• Multiplying by $i$ rotates $z$ $90^\circ$ counter-clockwise
• Taking the conjugate $z^*$ reflects $z$ across the real axis

💡 Worked Example — Geometry of Multiplication by $i$
Let $z = 2 - i$. Find $iz$ and describe the transformation.

  Step 1: Multiply
    $$iz = i(2 - i) = 2i - i^2 = 2i + 1 = 1 + 2i$$

  Step 2: Compare on the Argand diagram
    $z = 2 - i$ is at $(2, -1)$
    $iz = 1 + 2i$ is at $(1, 2)$

  Step 3: Describe
    The point has rotated $90^\circ$ counter-clockwise about the origin.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always sketch the point before deciding the quadrant for $\arg(z)$
• $\arg(0)$ is undefined — there is no angle to measure
• A negative argument simply means the angle is measured clockwise

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)$ directly without checking the quadrant. For example, $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{-1}{-1}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, but the correct argument for $-1 - i$ is $-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ because it lies in Q3.

notes.heading: Polar, Euler Forms & Operations
notes.body:
Polar and Euler forms package a complex number by its size (modulus) and direction (argument). These forms make multiplication, division, and powers almost effortless compared with Cartesian form.

📌 Polar (cis) Form
Any complex number can be written as:
    $$z = r(\cos \theta + i \sin \theta) = r \operatorname{cis} \theta$$
where:
    $$r = |z| \quad (\text{modulus})$$
    $$\theta = \arg(z) \quad (\text{argument})$$

📌 Euler (Exponential) Form
    $$z = r e^{i\theta}$$

This reveals a deep link between exponentials and trigonometry. It is equivalent to polar form and is ideal for multiplication, division, and powers.

🔑 Multiplication & Division in Polar/Euler Form
To multiply: multiply the moduli and add the arguments
    $$z_1 z_2 = r_1 r_2 \operatorname{cis}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$$

To divide: divide the moduli and subtract the arguments
    $$\dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2} \operatorname{cis}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)$$

If the new argument falls outside $-\pi < \theta \leq \pi$, add or subtract $2\pi$ to bring it back into range.

🔑 De Moivre's Theorem
For powers of a complex number in polar form:
    $$z^n = r^n \operatorname{cis}(n\theta)$$

💡 Worked Example — Multiplication in Polar Form
Let $z_1 = 3 \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ and $z_2 = 2 \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$. Find $z_1 z_2$.

  Step 1: Multiply the moduli
    $$r = 3 \times 2 = 6$$

  Step 2: Add the arguments
    $$\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{2\pi}{12} + \dfrac{3\pi}{12} = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}$$

  Step 3: Write the result
    $$z_1 z_2 = 6 \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\right)$$

💡 Worked Example — Conversion Between Forms
Express $z = 2 + 2i$ in polar form $r \operatorname{cis} \theta$.

  Step 1: Find the modulus
    $$r = \sqrt{2^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$$

  Step 2: Find the argument
    Point $(2, 2)$ is in Q1, so $\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{2}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

  Step 3: Write in polar form
    $$z = 2\sqrt{2} \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$$

💡 Worked Example — De Moivre's Theorem
Let $z = 2e^{i\pi/3}$. Calculate $z^2$.

  Step 1: Apply the theorem
    $$z^2 = 2^2 e^{i \cdot 2\pi/3} = 4e^{2\pi i/3}$$

  Step 2: Convert to Cartesian form (optional)
    $$4\left[\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) + i \sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)\right] = 4\left(-\dfrac{1}{2} + i \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -2 + 2\sqrt{3} \, i$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Polar/Euler forms are much faster than Cartesian form for multiplication and division
• Always check that the final argument lies in the required range
• The conjugate of $r \operatorname{cis} \theta$ is $r \operatorname{cis}(-\theta)$
• Euler's identity: $$e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$$ connects the five most important numbers in mathematics

⚠️ Common Mistake
Trying to add complex numbers in polar form by adding moduli and arguments. Addition only works cleanly in Cartesian form. Convert to $a + bi$ first, add, then convert back if needed.

notes.heading: De Moivre's Theorem & nth Roots
notes.body:
De Moivre's theorem turns raising a complex number to a power into simple arithmetic on the modulus and argument. It also leads to a neat formula for finding all nth roots of a complex number.

📌 De Moivre's Theorem
For a complex number in polar form $z = r \operatorname{cis} \theta$ and any integer $n$:
    $$z^n = r^n \operatorname{cis}(n\theta)$$

🔑 Key Idea
Raising $z$ to the $n$th power multiplies the argument by $n$ and raises the modulus to the $n$th power.

📌 nth Roots of a Complex Number
The $n$ distinct nth roots of $z = r \operatorname{cis} \theta$ are:
    $$z_k = r^{1/n} \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{\theta + 2k\pi}{n}\right)$$
where $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, n-1$.

🔑 How it works
1. Take the $n$th root of the modulus: $r^{1/n}$
2. Start with the principal argument $\theta$
3. Add multiples of $2\pi$ to $\theta$ and divide each by $n$
4. The $n$ roots are equally spaced around a circle of radius $r^{1/n}$

💡 Worked Example — Power using De Moivre
Let $z = 2 \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$. Find $z^3$.

  Step 1: Apply the theorem
    $$z^3 = 2^3 \operatorname{cis}\left(3 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$$

  Step 2: Simplify
    $$z^3 = 8 \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$$

  Step 3: Convert to Cartesian form
    $$8\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} + i \sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 8(0 + i) = 8i$$

💡 Worked Example — Cube Roots of Unity
Find the three cube roots of $1$.

  Step 1: Write $1$ in polar form
    $$1 = 1 \operatorname{cis}(0)$$

  Step 2: Apply the formula with $n = 3$ and $k = 0, 1, 2$
    $$z_k = 1^{1/3} \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{0 + 2k\pi}{3}\right)$$

  Step 3: List the roots
    $$z_0 = \operatorname{cis}(0) = 1$$
    $$z_1 = \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i$$
    $$z_2 = \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• De Moivre's theorem only applies directly to polar or Euler form
• There are always exactly $n$ distinct $n$th roots
• Roots of unity form a regular $n$-gon on the unit circle

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to add $2k\pi$ before dividing by $n$. Dividing $\theta$ by $n$ alone gives only the principal root and misses the others.

notes.heading: Polynomials with Complex Roots
notes.body:
When polynomial equations have real coefficients, their complex roots always come in conjugate pairs. This is one of the most useful facts for solving and factorising polynomials over the complex numbers.

📌 Conjugate Root Theorem
If a polynomial has real coefficients and $z = a + bi$ is a root, then its conjugate $z^* = a - bi$ is also a root.

🔑 Key Concept
The theorem guarantees symmetry: non-real roots appear in matching conjugate pairs whenever the polynomial's coefficients are real numbers.

🔑 Why it works
For real-coefficient polynomials, imaginary parts must cancel out in symmetric pairs. A single isolated complex root would force some coefficients to be non-real.

💡 Worked Example — Finding a Conjugate Root
Given that $2 + i$ is a root of $x^2 - 4x + 5 = 0$, find the other root.

  Step 1: Apply the theorem
    The conjugate of $2 + i$ is $2 - i$.

  Step 2: Verify (optional)
    $$[x - (2 + i)][x - (2 - i)] = (x - 2)^2 - i^2 = x^2 - 4x + 4 + 1 = x^2 - 4x + 5$$

  Answer: The other root is $2 - i$.

💡 Worked Example — Building a Polynomial from Roots
Find a real quadratic with roots $1 + 2i$ and $1 - 2i$.

  Step 1: Use the factor form
    $$[x - (1 + 2i)][x - (1 - 2i)]$$

  Step 2: Expand
    $$(x - 1)^2 - (2i)^2 = x^2 - 2x + 1 - 4i^2$$

  Step 3: Replace $i^2$ with $-1$
    $$x^2 - 2x + 1 + 4 = x^2 - 2x + 5$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The theorem only applies when all coefficients are real
• A degree-$n$ polynomial has exactly $n$ roots in $\mathbb{C}$ counting multiplicity
• If the degree is odd, there is always at least one real root

⚠️ Common Mistake
Assuming $3 + i$ and $-3 + i$ are conjugates. The conjugate of $3 + i$ is $3 - i$; only the sign of the imaginary part changes.

notes.heading: Loci in the Complex Plane
notes.body:
A locus is a set of points that satisfy a given condition. In the complex plane, simple equations involving $z$ describe familiar geometric shapes such as circles and lines.

📌 Definition of a Locus
A locus is the set of all points $z$ in the complex plane that satisfy a particular equation or inequality.

🔑 Common Loci

Circle centred at $a$ with radius $r$:
    $$|z - a| = r$$

Perpendicular bisector of the segment joining $a$ and $b$:
    $$|z - a| = |z - b|$$

Ray from the origin at angle $\alpha$:
    $$\arg(z) = \alpha$$

Region inside a circle:
    $$|z - a| < r$$

💡 Worked Example — Identifying a Locus
Describe the locus given by $|z - (2 + i)| = 3$.

  Step 1: Compare with the standard form
    $$|z - a| = r$$
    Here $a = 2 + i$ and $r = 3$.

  Step 2: Interpret
    This is a circle centred at $2 + i$ with radius $3$.

💡 Worked Example — Perpendicular Bisector
Describe the locus $|z - 1| = |z - i|$.

  Step 1: Recognise the form
    It states that the distance from $z$ to $1$ equals the distance from $z$ to $i$.

  Step 2: Identify the geometric shape
    The set of points equidistant from two fixed points is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.

  Step 3: Find the line
    The segment from $1$ to $i$ has midpoint $\dfrac{1 + i}{2}$ and slope $-1$, so the perpendicular bisector has slope $1$ and passes through the midpoint. Its equation is $y = x$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $|z - a| = r$ is a circle; $|z - a| < r$ is its interior
• $|z - a| = |z - b|$ is a straight line (perpendicular bisector)
• $\arg(z - a) = \alpha$ is a ray starting from $a$ at angle $\alpha$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing $|z - a|$ as $|z| - |a|$. Moduli do not distribute over subtraction. For example, $|3 + 4i - (1 + i)| = |2 + 3i| = \sqrt{13}$, not $|3 + 4i| - |1 + i| = 5 - \sqrt{2}$.

questions.stem: Find $\arg(z)$ for $z = -1 - i$, giving your answer in the range $-\pi < \theta \leq \pi$.
questions.explanation: $z$ lies in Q3. $\tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so the angle is $-\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.
$r = \sqrt{4 + 4} = 2\sqrt{2}$. The point $(2, -2)$ is in Q4, so $\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

questions.stem: Let $z_1 = 3 \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ and $z_2 = 2 \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$. Find $z_1 z_2$ in polar form.
Which geometric transformation represents multiplication by $i$?
questions.explanation: Multiplying by $i$ rotates a complex number $90^\circ$ counter-clockwise about the origin.
Multiply top and bottom by $1 + i$: $\dfrac{(2 + i)(1 + i)}{(1 - i)(1 + i)} = \dfrac{2 + 2i + i + i^2}{1 + 1} = \dfrac{1 + 3i}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{3}{2}i$.
Using De Moivre's theorem: $(\sqrt{2})^4 = 4$ and $4 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{8} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $z^4 = 4 \operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

questions.stem: Which of the following are the square roots of $-4$?
A real cubic polynomial has roots $1$ and $2 + i$. What is its third root?
questions.explanation: By the Conjugate Root Theorem, non-real roots of real polynomials occur in conjugate pairs, so the third root is $2 - i$.
